ABSTRACT
We present globally inverted pressure–temperature (P–T) phase diagrams up to 5,000
GPa for four fundamental planetary materials, Fe, MgO, SiO2, and MgSiO3, derived
from logistic regression and supervised learning, together with an experimental phase
equilibria database. These new P–T phase diagrams provide a solution to long-standing
disputes about their melting curves.
Their implications extend to the melting and
freezing of rocky materials in the interior of giant planets and super-Earth exoplanets,
contributing to the refinement of their internal structure models.

SiO2, and MgSiO3) and iron (Fe), except in the
context of studying the Earth’s interior (Liu
& Bassett 1986; Stixrude & Lithgow-Bertelloni
2011). However, these materials also constitute
the deep interiors of giant planets (Lewis 2004;
Mazevet et al. 2019) and exoplanets (Duffy et al.
2015).
The pressure–temperature (P–T) phase diagrams of these materials, especially their melting curves, remain poorly understood under
the relevant conditions of giant planets and
exoplanets.
The centers of giant planets in
our Solar System can reach pressures of 500–
5,000 GPa (Nettelmann et al. 2016; Mazevet
et al. 2019; Stixrude et al. 2021; Militzer &
Hubbard 2023, 2024; James & Stixrude 2024),
while super-Earth exoplanets have central pressures of up to 5,000 GPa at 10 Earth masses
(Stixrude 2014; Duffy et al. 2015; Boujibar et al.
2020). In contrast to the low melting temperature and relatively uniform fluid behavior of
hydrogen, rocky materials and iron metal are
relatively refractory between 1,000–5,000 GPa
(Root et al. 2015; Soubiran & Militzer 2020;
Hansen et al. 2021; Gonz´alez-Cataldo et al.
2016; Fei et al. 2021; Geng & Mohn 2024; Deng
et al. 2023; Morard et al. 2011; Stixrude 2012;
Kraus et al. 2022; Gonz´alez-Cataldo & Militzer
2023), and exhibits a wide range of exotic chemical behaviors at ultrahigh pressures potentially
as the core of gaint planets or the mantle of
super-Earth and sub-Neptune exoplanets, including the metallization of oxide solids (e.g.,
McWilliams et al. 2012), the diverse polymorphism of silicate solids (e.g., Umemoto et al.
2017), and the enhanced electrical conductivity
of the silicate liquid (Dragulet & Stxirude 2023;
Lherm et al. 2024). These results highlight the
profound implications of solid-solid phase transitions and melting in the interiors of giant planets and exoplanets.
Previous efforts to directly determine the P–
T phase boundaries of rocks and iron have typically focused on one phase boundary at a time,
using a single set of phase equilibrium data consisting of 10–100 points near the phase boundary to bracket the transition (e.g. Chanyshev
et al. 2022). Alternatively, equations of state
for the materials are determined experimentally
and then combined with extrapolated thermodynamic properties, such as enthalpy (∆H) and
entropy (∆S), to construct a thermodynamic
model of their phase equilibria (e.g. Stixrude &
Lithgow-Bertelloni 2011; Kojitani et al. 2016).

approach often rely on visual inspection and
freehand drawing based on a small data set and
do not directly show interlaboratory discrepancies; the topology of the phase equilibria computed by the latter approach is very sensitive to
the choice of thermodynamic parameters, which
are often measured experimentally only at low
temperatures and pressures and then extrapolated to the pressure and temperature ranges of
planetary interiors (Kojitani et al. 2016).

2. METHODS
2.1. Phase Equilibria Database
We have compiled a comprehensive phase
equilibria database for Fe, MgO, SiO2, and
MgSiO3, including a wide range of experimental and theoretical data produced over ∼80
years, from the early 1940s to the present.
The database includes ∼3,300 entries for Fe,
∼1,100 for MgO, ∼1,600 for SiO2, and ∼800
for MgSiO3. The data are categorized into three
main types:
1. Experimental data from static compression techniques, such as multi-anvil press
(MA) and diamond anvil cell (DAC) (Ito
2007; Mao et al. 2018);
2. Experimental data from dynamic compression techniques, such as gas gun compression and laser and magnetic pulse
compression (Duffy & Smith 2019);
3. Computationally-simulated
data
from
first-principles
quantum
mechanical
methods, such as density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations as
well as quantum Monte Carlo (QMC)
simulations (Wentzcovitch & Stixrude
2010).
Most of the data entries are compiled from
experimental observations of phase equilibria
in static compression experiments, and among
them we further distinguish two main types:
1. Direct observations: crossing of a phase
transition or reaction boundary;
2. Indirect observations: identification of a
stable phase.
Direct observations involve the identification
of a phase transition or reaction in a single experiment. We note that such observations can
be influenced by kinetic barriers, making it difficult to unambiguously identify the equilibrium
phase boundaries. For example, the sluggish kinetics of MgSiO3 at low temperature often leads
to conflicting observations of its transition or
reaction boundary (Kuroda et al. 2000), and
therefore we only include data collected >1,000
K to ensure reliable interpretation of these observations (Section 3.4).
Indirect observations involve the identification
of a phase at a given P–T without crossing
a phase transition or reaction boundary.
For
example, experimental data of the equation of
state of a single phase may not directly inform
us of its phase equilibrium (e.g. Pigott et al.
2015), but they contain valuable information
about the P–T conditions at which its polymorphs are likely to be not stable. While these
phases provide valuable information, they do
not guarantee that the observed phase is the
stable phase under the given conditions.
A
notorious example is SiO2, whose metastable
phases are very common and often persist at
low temperatures well beyond the expected
phase boundary (Prakapenka et al. 2004; Akaogi
2022). Careful consideration must therefore be
given to which data sets to include. Those with
clear evidence of metastable phases are excluded
from our inversion.
In addition, we also include some miscellaneous measurements, such
as experimental data on the physical properties

4
of the Fe liquid (e.g. Ohta et al. 2016), which,
although not primarily focused on determining
the melting curve, provide additional information on the conditions under which the solid
phase is likely not stable.
These indirect observations, which have not
historically been used to construct P–T phase
diagrams, are not, in our view, ancillary to direct observations of phase transitions. On the
contrary, the statistical framework we build here
uses information about both the conditions under which a phase is stable and those under
which it is not (see details in Section 2.2).
Furthermore, melting experiments sometimes
only report the “incipient melting” temperature, which is the lowest temperature at which
this detection method could identify liquid (e.g.
Zhang et al. 2016).
We include these data
only if they are reported with uncertainties, and
we treat each “incipient melting” temperature
as two data points, using the lower temperature limit of the uncertainty range as the lower
bound and the upper temperature limit as the upper
bound. For example, if an experimental report
states that “the melting point is between 1,200
K and 1,500 K”, we use two points: (1,200 K,
Tm) and (1,500 K, Tm). This approach allows
us to incorporate the full range of possible Tm
values into our analysis, while avoiding the
need for an explicit lower bound (e.g., Tm ≥ 1,200 K). We also include a small number of
cases where the melting point is above 5,000
GPa (e.g., the case of Fe at 1,000 GPa, 1,500
K, which is an extrapolation beyond the data
provided by the experimentalists and is thus
not treated as a direct data point).
The database also includes data from experimental
and theoretical studies across a wide range
of pressures and temperatures, providing a
robust foundation for our inversion.

pressures and then extrapolated to the pressure
and temperature ranges of planetary interiors (Kojitani et al. 2016).
